'''''Helosciadium repens''''', commonly known as '''creeping marshwort''',<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://bomax.botany.pl/ib-db/check/ |title=Vascular plants of Poland: a checklist = Krytyczna lista roślin naczyniowych Polski |date=1995 |publisher=Polish Academy of Sciences, W. Szafer Institute of Botany |isbn=978-83-85444-38-1 |editor-last=Mirek |editor-first=Zbigniew |series=Polish botanical studies |location=Kraków, Poland |language= |editor-last2=Bernacki |editor-first2=Leszek |editor-last3=Instytut Botaniki im. W. Szafera}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Gawryś |first=Wiesław |title=Słownik roślin zielnych: łacińsko-polski |date=2008 |publisher=Officina Botanica |isbn=978-83-925110-5-2 |location=Kraków |page=27}}</ref> is a [[species]] of plant belonging to the [[Apiaceae]] family.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Szafer|1960|pp=57-59}}</ref> It occurs in Western and Central [[Europe]], being rare throughout its range. It grows in wetland areas where it does not have to compete with taller plants due to grazing by animals, periodic flooding during the winter-spring seasons, or mowing. It is considered a species of [[Near-threatened species|near-threatened]] status at the continental level, [[Critically Endangered|critically endangered]] and legally protected in Poland. It is subject to protection within the European [[Natura 2000]] network.

== Geographical distribution ==
The creeping marshwort is a subatlantic species. It grows in Western Europe from the [[Iberian Peninsula]] to the [[British Isles]] and [[Denmark]] in the north, as well as [[Poland]], [[Slovakia]], [[Hungary]], [[Croatia]], and [[Montenegro]] in the east. Isolated occurrences outside its core range are found in [[Turkey]], [[Morocco]], and the [[Canary Islands]].<ref name="npgsweb">{{Cite web |title=Helosciadium repens (Jacq.) W. D. J. Koch |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomydetail?id=464223 |access-date=2024-04-08 |website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov |publisher=Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN-Taxonomy)}}</ref> As a naturalized species, it has been reported from the [[Czech Republic]],<ref name="npgsweb" /> [[North America]],<ref>{{Cite book |title=Polska czerwona księga roślin: paprotniki i rośliny kwiatowe |date=2014 |publisher=Instytut Ochrony Przyrody. Polska Akademia Nauk |isbn=978-83-61191-72-8 |editor-last=Kaźmierczakowa |editor-first=Róża |edition=3 |location=Kraków |pages=360–362 |editor-last2=Mirek |editor-first2=Zbigniew |editor-last3=Zarzycki |editor-first3=Kazimierz}}</ref> and even from the [[Swartland]] region in the [[Western Cape]] province of [[South Africa]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sonder |first=W. |url=https://plants.jstor.org/stable/10.5555/al.ap.flora.floc004904 |title=Flora Capensis |year=1894 |volume=2 |page=524}}</ref>

Throughout its range, the species is rarely encountered,<ref name="Burmeier-2008">{{Cite journal |last1=Burmeier |first1=Sandra |last2=Jensen |first2=Kai |year=2008 |title=Is the endangered Apium repens (Jacq.) Lag. rare because of a narrow regeneration niche? |url=https://esj-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1442-1984.2008.00212.x |journal=Plant Species Biology |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=111–118|doi=10.1111/j.1442-1984.2008.00212.x |bibcode=2008PSBio..23..111B |url-access=subscription }}</ref> influenced by both its specific ecological requirements and its poor ability to spread over long distances.<ref name="Jansen">{{Cite web |last1=Jansen |first1=Kai |last2=Schwerstfeger |first2=Jan |last3=Burmeier |first3=Sandra |title=Conservation guideline for Apium repens |url=https://www.life-baltcoast.de/fileadmin/user_upload/Conservation_guideline_Apium_repens-05_04_11.pdf |access-date=2019-08-04 |website=Universitat Hamburg |publisher=EU-Life Project Baltcoast}}</ref> In the southern part of its range, it grows in mountainous areas (e.g., in [[Spain]]<ref name="Loidi-2017">{{Cite book |last=Loidi |first=Javier |title=The vegetation of the Iberian Peninsula |date=2017 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-54867-8 |series=Plant and vegetation |location=Cham |page=379}}</ref> and Morocco, at altitudes above {{convert|2300|m|-1}} above sea level).<ref name="McDonald-2006">{{Cite web |last1=McDonald |first1=A. W. |last2=Lambrick |first2=C. R. |year=2006 |title=Apium repens creeping marshwort. Species Recovery Programme 1995-2005 |url=http://publications.naturalengland.org.uk/file/86042 |access-date=2019-08-04 |website=English Nature |publisher=English Nature Research Reports}}</ref>

== Morphology ==
[[File:Helosciadium repens sl39.jpg|thumb|Shoot of creeping marshwort]]
[[File:Helosciadium repens kz25.jpg|thumb|Umbella with flowers]]

=== Habit ===
The naked, shiny [[perennial]] with creeping [[Stolon|stolons]] typically reaches {{Convert abbreviated|10-20|cm}} in terrestrial habitats, sometimes up to {{Convert abbreviated|50|cm}}<ref name="Chmiel-2012">{{Cite journal |last1=Chmiel |first1=J. |last2=Ziarnek |first2=K. |year=2012 |editor-last=Perzanowska |editor-first=J. |title=Monitoring gatunków roślin. Przewodnik metodyczny. Część druga |journal=Biblioteka Monitoringu Środowiska |publisher=GIOŚ |pages=243–259}}</ref> or {{Convert abbreviated|60|cm}},<ref name="Landesamt für Umweltschutz Sachsen-Anhalt">{{Cite web |title=Kriechender Sumpfsellerie Helosciadium repens (Jacq.) W.D.J. Koch |url=https://lau.sachsen-anhalt.de/fileadmin/Bibliothek/Politik_und_Verwaltung/MLU/LAU/Naturschutz/Natura2000/Arten_und_Lebensraumtypen/Dateien/Artensteckbrief_Helosciadium_repens.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190805072134/https://lau.sachsen-anhalt.de/fileadmin/Bibliothek/Politik_und_Verwaltung/MLU/LAU/Naturschutz/Natura2000/Arten_und_Lebensraumtypen/Dateien/Artensteckbrief_Helosciadium_repens.pdf |archive-date=2019-08-05 |access-date=2019-08-05 |website=Landesamt für Umweltschutz Sachsen-Anhalt}}</ref> and when growing in water, even up to {{Convert abbreviated|1|m|ft}}<ref name="Bojňanský-2007">{{Cite book |last1=Bojňanský |first1=Vít |title=Atlas of seeds and fruits of Central and East-European flora: the Carpathian Mountains Region |last2=Fargašová |first2=Agáta |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4020-5361-0 |location=Dordrecht |page=447}}</ref> or {{Convert abbreviated|1.5|m|ft}}<ref name="Landesamt für Umweltschutz Sachsen-Anhalt" /> in length. In the nodes, the stolons root and develop leaves, which are sometimes absent in the node from which the flower stalk emerges. There are no erect and leafy stems.<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> The roots are filamentous. The [[Plant stem|stem]] is light green, smooth, and naked.<ref name="Sell-2009">{{Cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter D. |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge university press |isbn=978-0-521-55337-7 |volume=3 |location=Cambridge |page=291}}</ref>

=== Leaves ===
They grow from the nodes of the stolons, reaching up to {{Convert abbreviated|10|cm}}, sometimes up to {{Convert abbreviated|20|cm}} in length<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> (in plants submerged in water, even up to 40 cm),<ref name="Verband Botanischen Garten">{{Cite web |title=Helosciadium repens (Kriechender Sellerie) |url=http://www.ex-situ-erhaltung.de/pflanzenarten/h/helosciadium-repens/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160810203500/http://www.ex-situ-erhaltung.de/pflanzenarten/h/helosciadium-repens/ |archive-date=2016-08-10 |access-date=2019-11-25 |website=Verband Botanischen Garten |publisher=Ex-Situ-Erhaltung}}</ref> but most often only up to 5 cm in length and 1.5 cm in width.<ref name="Sell-2009" /> The [[Leaf sheath|leaf sheaths]] are inconspicuous.<ref name="van Moorsel">{{Cite web |last=van Moorsel |first=René |title=Apium repens (Jacquin) Lag. |url=https://www.verspreidingsatlas.nl/0079 |access-date=2024-04-08 |website=Verspreidingsatlas |publisher=FLORON Verspreidingsatlas Vaatplanten |language=nl-nl}}</ref> The leaf blades are attached to long petioles and are individually, odd-pinnately compound.<ref name="Szafer">{{Harvard citation text|Szafer|1960|p=58}}</ref> The leaflets, numbering 3–6 pairs,<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> are sessile, ovate to rounded, with unevenly and coarsely toothed margins.<ref name="Szafer" /> They reach up to 1 cm in length.<ref name="Sell-2009" /> One of the notches between the teeth, especially on the third pair of leaflets from the bottom, is distinctly deeper, which is a significant diagnostic feature distinguishing this species from terrestrial forms of [[fool's watercress]].<ref name="McDonald-2006" /> The leaves are usually yellowish-green, lighter underneath, and naked.<ref name="Sell-2009" />

=== Flowers ===
Gathered in [[umbellules]] arising from the node of the creeping stem, the umbels, along with their peduncles, reach a height of {{Convert abbreviated|1-3.5|cm|4=1}},<ref name="Rutkowski-2004">{{Cite book |last=Rutkowski |first=Lucjan |title=Klucz do oznaczania roślin naczyniowych Polski niżowej |date=2004 |publisher=Wydaw. Naukowe PWN |isbn=978-83-01-14342-8 |edition=2 |location=Warsaw}}</ref> maximum up to {{Convert abbreviated|10|cm}}, sometimes {{Convert abbreviated|15|cm}}.<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> The umbel consists of 2–7 umbellules, each supported by numerous, white-bordered, elliptic, and three-veined [[bracteoles]].<ref name="Szafer" /> The pedicels of the umbellules are usually longer than the pedicels of the flowers, although they may be strongly shortened on heavily grazed pastures.<ref name="Stroh-2016">{{Cite web |last1=Stroh |first1=P. A. |last2=Webb |first2=J. |last3=Rumsey |first3=F. J. |year=2016 |title=Apium repens (Jacq.) Lag. Creeping Marshwort. Species account |url=https://bsbi.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/Apium_repens_species_account.pdf |access-date=2019-07-30 |website=Botanical Society of Britain & Ireland}}</ref> At the base of the umbel peduncle, there are usually 3 to 7 quickly shedding, lanceolate [[Bract|bracts]].<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> The flowers are small, with white (sometimes cream or pinkish)<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> corolla petals reaching about 0.5 mm in length, mostly with a pointed and inwardly bent tip.<ref name="Piękoś-Mirkowa-2006">{{Cite book |last1=Piękoś-Mirkowa |first1=Halina |title=Rośliny chronione |last2=Mirek |first2=Zbigniew |date=2006 |publisher=Multico Oficyna Wydawnicza |isbn=978-83-7073-444-2 |edition=2 |series=Flora Polski |location=Warszawa |page=22}}</ref> [[Sepal]]s are absent. There are 5 [[Stamen|stamens]] with white filaments and pale yellow [[anthers]]. The [[pistil]]s are two, bent in two directions. The [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]] is small and capitate. The pistils are seated on a stylopodium reaching half their length.<ref name="Sell-2009" />

=== Fruits ===
The spherical [[Schizocarp|schizocarps]] have a length of 1–1.3 mm and a width of 1.1–1.4 mm<ref name="Bojňanský-2007" /> (the schizocarp is slightly wider than it is long), with persistent styles bent at the apex.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> The size of the fruits is influenced by the plant's growth conditions – they are larger under optimal conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Florkowski |first=Krystian |date=2018-02-09 |title=Morphological variability of fruits in Apium repens (Jacq.) Lag. – a critically endangered species in Poland |url=http://www1.up.poznan.pl/steciana/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/steciana-21-09.pdf |journal=Steciana |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=85–92 |doi=10.12657/steciana.021.009}}</ref> Individual schizocarps are bluntly 5-angled in cross-section with weakly marked ribs.<ref name="Szafer" /> The fruit mass is 0.27 ± 0.04 mg.<ref name="Verband Botanischen Garten" />

=== Similar species ===
The creeping marshwort can be confused with common young specimens of the [[lesser water-parsnip]] (''Berula erecta'') and the [[Sium latifolium|great water-parsnip]] (''Sium latifolium''), which grow in similar habitats. However, the flowering stems of these species are erect and leafy, with the inflorescences almost sessile (in contrast, the stems of creeping marshwort are always prostrate, and the inflorescences are elevated on stalks several centimeters long). Very similar is the [[fool's watercress]] (''Helosciadium nodiflorum''), which, however, has a maximum of two bracts and shorter stalks of umbels compared to the stalks of umbellules.<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> This species, in its terrestrial form, can coexist with creeping marshwort in meadows and can be almost indistinguishable to such an extent that genetic research is necessary to determine the taxonomic affiliation of the plants.<ref name="Grassly-1996">{{Cite journal |last1=Grassly |first1=N. C. |last2=Harris |first2=S. A. |last3=Cronk |first3=Q. C. B |year=1996 |title=British Apium repens (Jacq.) Lag. (Apiaceae) status assessed using random amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD) |url=http://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Wats21p103.pdf |journal=Watsonia |volume=21 |pages=103–111}}</ref> Another similar species, ''{{Interlanguage link|Helosciadium inundatum|pl|Pęczyna wodna}}'', lacks bracts altogether, and its leaflets have wedge-shaped bases, not rounded as in creeping marshworts.<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /><gallery mode="packed">

== Biology ==
[[File:Apium repens kz04.jpg|thumb|Seedling of creeping marshwort]]
[[File:Helosciadium repens kz01.jpg|thumb|Node with developing leaves]]
[[File:Helosciadium repens kz02.jpg|thumb|Stolon of creeping marshwort]]
[[File:Helosciadium repens kz09.jpg|thumb|Fruiting creeping marshwort]]

=== Development ===
The creeping marshwort can be classified as a [[hemicryptophyte]], [[helophyte]], or [[hydrophyte]] depending on the habitat conditions.<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> Among plants with a [[molecular cloning]] type, creeping marshwort is included in the ''[[Fragaria vesca]]'' group characterized by the predominance of spreading through stolons with relatively short individual [[ramet]] lifespans.<ref name="Rosenthal-2008">{{Cite journal |last1=Rosenthal |first1=Gert |last2=Lederbogen |first2=Dirk |year=2008 |title=Response of the clonal plant Apium repens (Jacq.) Lag. to extensive grazing |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0367253007001326 |journal=Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=203 |issue=2 |pages=141–151|doi=10.1016/j.flora.2007.02.004 |bibcode=2008FMDFE.203..141R |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Flowering occurs from June to October,<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> with [[self-pollination]] playing a significant role.<ref name="Herden-2019">{{Cite web |last1=Herden |first1=T. |last2=Bönisch |first2=T. |last3=Friesen |first3=N. |year=2019 |title=Genetische Erhaltungsgebiete für Helosciadium repens (Jacq.) W.D.J.Koch |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333641005 |access-date=2019-08-04 |website=Fachtagung "Genetische Erhaltungsgebiete für Wildpflanzen für Ernährung und Landwirtschaft – ein neues Modul zur Stärkung des Artenschutzes", Quedlinburg, Deutschland, 04.-05.06.2019}}</ref> Fruits ripen from August to October.<ref name="Verband Botanischen Garten" />

In Central Europe, it is assumed that the species primarily reproduces vegetatively through stolons.<ref name="Chmiel-2012" /> On the other hand, studies on seed germination ecology suggest that, contrary to previous beliefs, at least in northern Germany, there are no significant problems or limitations for the species to spread via seeds.<ref name="Burmeier-2008" /> A complicating factor for generative reproduction may be excessive turf density and the lack of initial microsites free from vegetation.<ref name="GIO">{{Cite web |year=2015 |title=Selery błotne Apium repens (1614) |url=http://siedliska.gios.gov.pl/images/pliki_pdf/wyniki/2013-2014/dla_roslin/Selery-botne-Apium-repens.pdf |website=Monitoring gatunków i siedlisk przyrodniczych ze szczególnym uwzględnieniem specjalnych obszarów ochrony siedlisk Natura 2000 |publisher=Główny Inspektorat Ochrony Środowiska}}</ref>

The seeds have the ability to float in water for at least 50 days without losing their germination capacity, which is significant for their dispersal ([[hydrochory]]). They can be carried by water over long distances (in lake basins or along streams), but they can also be moved on a smaller scale within grassland communities during periodic floods, for example, after heavy rains.<ref name="Burmeier-2008" /> Outside of water, the fruits are transported by wind and animals, both attached to fur and hooves ([[epizoochory]]) and consumed ([[endozoochory]]).<ref name="Verband Botanischen Garten" />

Seeds partially germinate in the same season they mature, even those floating in water.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> The seeds form a persistent [[soil seed bank]], retaining the ability to germinate when buried in the soil<ref name="Burmeier-2008" /> (even up to 70 years).<ref name="GIO" /> The density of seeds on species' habitats is recorded at about a thousand seeds per square meter.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> Seed [[germination]] occurs under a wide range of abiotic conditions. In terms of temperature, germination is limited only by high temperatures, which rarely occur in habitats wet and humid enough for the species. It thrives in variable temperatures, although it is not necessary. Good light conditions are necessary for germination. Seeds germinate well on moist substrate, even when flooded for two weeks, which usually limits competition from other species (in places where water stagnates, seeds of most species enter a dormant phase).<ref name="Burmeier-2008" />

Creeping marshwort populations exhibit large fluctuations in the number of individuals depending on prevailing water conditions or other interactions, such as grazing.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /><ref name="Rosenthal-2008" /> In locations on pastures, plants may seemingly disappear during periods of intense cattle grazing, only to quickly recolonize gaps in the sward during breaks in grazing. Naked patches of soil exposed by the trampling of wet soil by cows' hooves are significant for maintaining creeping marshwort on pastures. Due to the length of the stolons, these plants utilize gaps in the sward up to 10–15 cm away from them. For creeping marshwort to persist on pastures, grazing frequency is important – too infrequent grazing results in strong development of vegetation competing with this species and, consequently, its decline.<ref name="Rosenthal-2008" />

=== Genetics ===
The [[chromosome]] number is 2n=22.<ref name="Rutkowski-2004" /> A low genetic diversity within populations was observed, particularly in the lowland (northern) part of [[Germany]], while in the southern part of the country ([[Bavaria]]), the differentiation between populations was slightly higher.<ref name="Herden-2019" />

== Ecology ==
[[File:Apium repens kz06.jpg|thumb|Creeping marshwort in a pasture on Lake [[Miedwie]] in [[Poland]]]]
[[File:Helosciadium repens sl9.jpg|thumb|Creeping marshwort on a low-mowed lawn in [[Vienna]]]]

=== Habitat ===
Creeping marshwort is a light-demanding<ref name="Verband Botanischen Garten" /> [[pioneer species]] on wet, [[nitrogen]]-rich soil.<ref name="van Moorsel" /> It occurs along water edges, especially lakeshores, in communities of low vegetation flooded outside the growing season, and in gaps in [[Reed bed|reed beds]].<ref name="GIO" /><ref name="Jansen" /> Another primary habitat is small depressions in the terrain, flooded in the spring and later drying out,<ref name="Burmeier-2008" /><ref name="Rosenthal-2008" /> in the [[Netherlands]] also interdune depressions on the seaside.<ref name="van Moorsel" /> In places flooded in winter and spring, the bare soil surface is exposed after the water level drops, enabling the development of light-demanding creeping marshwort. Grazing by animals also favors its growth by chewing up competitive vegetation.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> Secondary habitats are [[Pasture|pastures]], usually extensive (over 50 ha), where [[cattle]] are extensively grazed,<ref name="Rosenthal-2008" /> sometimes also [[Horse|horses]],<ref name="Grassly-1996" /> as well as places trampled on the edges of waters, e.g., on beaches and boat launching sites,<ref name="Sýkora-1985">{{Cite journal |last1=Sýkora |first1=K. V. |last2=Westhoff |first2=V. |year=1985 |title=Synecology and syntaxonomy of Apium repens (Jacq.) Lag. & Scirpus cariciformis Vest., in particular in the eastern part of Zeeuws-Vlaanderen (Province of Zeeland, the Netherlands) |url=https://library.wur.nl/WebQuery/wurpubs/fulltext/459518 |journal=Tuexenia |volume=5 |pages=41–57}}</ref> and within recreational areas, including those landscaped as [[Lawn|lawns]].<ref name="GIO" /><ref name="Jansen" /> However, excessive trampling and grazing by animals can eliminate this species.<ref name="GIO" /><ref name="Rosenthal-2008" />

These plants inhabit fertile,<ref name="Piękoś-Mirkowa-2006" /> moderately fertile, and poor soils,<ref name="Sýkora-1985" /><ref name="van Moorsel" /> rich in nitrogen compounds,<ref name="van Moorsel" /> neutral to slightly acidic<ref name="Sýkora-1985" /><ref name="van Moorsel" /> or slightly alkaline.<ref name="Jansen" /> The mechanical and chemical composition of soils varies at different sites.<ref name="Jansen" /> A constant feature of habitats is the near-neutral [[soil pH]]<ref name="Jansen" /> and high humidity<ref name="Sýkora-1985" /><ref name="van Moorsel" /> (although often with a significant drop in water level by the end of summer).<ref name="Jansen" /> The species' habitats are periodically flooded or inundated with water for a longer period.<ref name="Piękoś-Mirkowa-2006" /><ref name="van Moorsel" /> In particular, places flooded in winter are preferred.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mennema |first1=J. |title=Atlas of the Netherlands Flora: Extinct and very rare species |last2=Quene-Boterenbrood |first2=A. J. |last3=Plate |first3=C. L. |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |year=2013 |isbn=978-94-009-9191-0 |page=51}}</ref> While these plants tolerate winter flooding well, prolonged submergence in the summer can lead to plant death<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> (plants die when flooded for more than 56 days<ref name="Burmeier-2009">{{Cite journal |last1=Burmeier |first1=Sandra |last2=Jensen |first2=Kai |date=2009-06-10 |title=Experimental ecology and habitat specificity of the endangered plant Apium repens (Jacq.) Lag. at the northern edge of its range |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/17550870902773658 |journal=Plant Ecology & Diversity |language=en |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=65–75 |doi=10.1080/17550870902773658 |bibcode=2009PlEcD...2...65B |issn=1755-0874|url-access=subscription }}</ref> or repeatedly inundated for shorter periods).<ref name="Jansen" /> These plants can tolerate shorter and less frequent floods, losing their roots and floating on the water surface.<ref name="McDonald-2006" /> However, creeping marshwort growing in water does not flower.<ref name="Verband Botanischen Garten" /> Submergence of the species' habitats in the summer stimulates seed germination.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> However, these plants wither when watered with saltwater,<ref name="Jansen" /> although sometimes they grow on slightly saline coastal alluvia.<ref name="McDonald-2006" />

Due to the pioneer character of the species, a constant feature of its occupied sites is the high frequency and intensity of interactions leading to the limited development of competitive vegetation.<ref name="Jansen" /> The habitat characteristics conditioning the development of creeping marshwort include low vegetation height (optimally not exceeding 20 cm) or at least the presence of gaps (e.g., in reed beds), lack of shading caused by trees and shrubs, and absence of competitive expansive species (strongly growing ones).<ref name="GIO" />

The plants tolerate frosts down to -20°C.<ref name="Verband Botanischen Garten" />

=== Phytosociology and interspecies interactions ===
[[File:Entyloma helosciadii kz02.jpg|thumb|Leaf of creeping marshwort infested with ''Entyloma helosciadii'' fungus]]
Creeping marshwort grows in Central Europe in communities of floodplain meadows from the ''Lolio-Potentillion anserinae'' association (''Agropyro-Rumicion crispi''), usually species-poor, as well as in richer communities of ''Triglochino-Agrostietum stoloniferae'' and ''Ranunculo-Alopecuretum geniculati''.<ref name="Sýkora-1985" /> The most common accompanying species of creeping marshwort (growing with them on over 50% of sites in northern Germany) include: [[Agrostis stolonifera|creeping bentgrass]] (''Agrostis stolonifera''), [[Ranunculus repens|creeping buttercup]] (''Ranunculus repens''), [[Argentina anserina|silverweed]] (''Potentilla anserina''), [[Mentha aquatica|water mint]] (''Mentha aquatica''), [[Juncus articulatus|jointleaf rush]] (''Juncus articulatus''), [[Carex hirta|hairy sedge]] (''Carex hirta''), [[Trifolium repens|white clover]] (''Trifolium repens''), [[Galium palustre|common marsh bedstraw]] (''Galium palustre''), and [[Poa pratensis|Kentucky bluegrass]] (''Poa pratensis'').<ref name="Jansen" />

In the [[British Isles]], creeping marshwort is recorded in grass communities dominated by [[Agrostis stolonifera|creeping bentgrass]] (''Agrostis stolonifera'') and [[Alopecurus geniculatus|water foxtail]] (''Alopecurus geniculatus'') and [[Ranunculus repens|creeping buttercup]] (''Ranunculus repens''), as well as in trampled grasslands of [[Poa annua|annual meadow grass]] (''Poa annua'') and [[Plantago major|broadleaf plantain]] (''Plantago major''). Alongside dominants in these communities, the most common species include: [[water mint]] (''Mentha aquatica''), [[Galium palustre|common marsh bedstraw]] (''Galium palustre''), [[Myosotis scorpioides|true forget-me-not]] (''Myosotis scorpioides''), [[Rorippa amphibia|great yellow-cress]] (''Rorippa palustris''), and [[Veronica scutellata|marsh speedwell]] (''Veronica scutellata'').<ref name="Stroh-2016" />

In [[France]], the species is indicated as associated with the association of ''Hydrocotylo vulgaris-Baldellion ranunculoidis'' communities, with vegetation typical of the shores of oligotrophic reservoirs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Helosciadium repens (Jacq.) W.D.J.Koch |url=https://www.tela-botanica.org/eflore/ |access-date=2024-04-08 |website=Tela Botanica |language=fr-FR}}</ref> On the [[Iberian Peninsula]], creeping marshwort grows on the banks of mountain streams accompanied by ''Glyceria declinata''.<ref name="Loidi-2017" />

Grazing of creeping marshwort by herbivorous animals (e.g., cattle in pastures) may affect the condition of plants, hinder their development, including fruit formation, but it benefits the population and ensures its sustainability by limiting the development of competitive vegetation and creating microhabitats optimal for this species. This, in turn, enables the spread of creeping marshwort in pastures independently of microhabitats shaped solely by the influence of water conditions – without grazing, creeping marshwort retreats, and its distribution is limited only to local depressions.<ref name="Jansen" />

Creeping marshwort leaves are readily consumed by [[Snail|snails]]<ref name="Stroh-2016" /><ref name="Grassly-1996" /> and [[Duck|ducks]].<ref name="Jansen" /> In [[Morocco]], they are fed upon by [[Barbary macaque|Barbary macaques]].<ref name="Grassly-1996" /> Plants are also sometimes seriously attacked by [[Aphid|aphids]] feeding on both leaves, root necks and roots.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> In [[Poland|Polish]] sites, no feeding on plants by invertebrates or signs of disease affecting the population have been observed.<ref name="GIO" />

== Systematics and variability ==
The species represents the genus ''[[Helosciadium]]'', which includes all European species formerly classified in the genus ''[[Apium]]'' except for its [[type species]] –  [[celeriac]] (''Apium graveolens'').<ref name="Ronse-2010" /> Traditionally, the genus ''Helosciadium'' was classified as a section within ''Apium'' for much of the 20th century, resulting in widespread use of the scientific name attributing it to this genus in the literature.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Les |first=Donald H. |title=Aquatic Dicotyledons of North America: Ecology, Life History, and Systematics |publisher=CRC Press |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-351-64440-2}}</ref> However, the separate genus ''Helosciadium'' is well supported by molecular, morphological,<ref name="Spalik-2009">{{Cite journal |last1=Spalik |first1=Krzysztof |last2=Downie |first2=Stephen R. |last3=Watson |first3=Mark F. |year=2009 |title=Generic delimitations within the Sium alliance (Apiaceae tribe Oenantheae) inferred from cpDNA rps16-5′trnK(UUU) and nrDNA ITS sequences |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/tax.583004 |journal= Taxon|volume=58 |issue=3 |pages=735–748|doi=10.1002/tax.583004 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Ronse-2010" /> and chemical analyses.<ref name="Ronse-2010" /> This genus belongs to the tribe ''Oenantheae'', closely related to ''[[Berula]]'' and ''[[Sium]]'',<ref name="Spalik-2009" /><ref name="Fröberg">{{Cite web |last=Fröberg |first=Lars |title=Helosciadium |url=http://www.floranordica.org/Review/-Review_public/accounts/Helosciadium.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221015030/http://www.floranordica.org/Review/-Review_public/accounts/Helosciadium.html |archive-date=2016-12-21 |access-date=2019-08-03 |url-status=usurped |website=Flora Nordica}}</ref> while the ''Apium'' genus represents another tribe – ''Apieae''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tribe Apieae |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomyfamily?type=tribe&id=3019 |access-date=2024-04-08 |website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov}}</ref><ref name="Ronse-2010" />

Within the genus, the species is most closely related to [[Helosciadium nodiflorum|fool's watercress]] (''Helosciadium nodiflorum''), with which it forms a [[sister group]] relative to three species: ''{{Interlanguage link|Helosciadium inundatum|pl|Pęczyna wodna}}'', ''Helosciadium'' ''crassipes'', and ''Helosciadium'' ''bermejoi''.<ref name="Ronse-2010" /><ref name="Spalik-2009" />

Under the name ''Apium'' × ''longipedunculatum'', a [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] with [[Helosciadium nodiflorum|fool's watercress]] (''Helosciadium nodiflorum'') has been described, confirmed in genetic studies.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> This hybrid differs from ''Helosciadium'' ''nodiflorum'' in having a creeping and more strongly rooting stem at the nodes. In some locations where parent specimens grew together, only this hybrid remained after creeping marshwort disappeared.<ref name="Sell-2009" /> Earlier, based solely on morphological observations, such a hybrid was also described (as ''Apium'' × ''riddelsdellii'' <small>Druce</small>), but the diagnosis from 1917 is considered doubtful<ref name="Grassly-1996" /> (at the site, a morphologically very similar intergeneric hybrid between ''Helosciadium'' ''nodiflorum'' and [[Berula erecta|lesser water-parsnip]] (''Berula erecta'') – × ''Beruladium'' – was also observed contemporarily, in addition to similar parent taxa).<ref name="Stroh-2016" />

== Nomenclature ==
The species was first scientifically described as ''Sium repens'' by [[Nikolaus Joseph von Jacquin]] in his work ''Flora Austriaca'', published in 1775. Subsequently, Mariano Lagasca y Segura described the species as a representative of the ''Apium'' genus under the name ''Apium repens'' (Jacq.) Lag. (1821), and three years later, it was classified by Johann F.W. Koch as ''Helosciadium repens'' (Jacq.) W.D.J. Koch (1824), a classification currently considered appropriate from a systematic standpoint.<ref name="Fröberg" /><ref name="Spalik-2009" /><ref name="Ronse-2010" /> However, in 1867, [[Heinrich Gustav Reichenbach]] again placed species from the genus ''Helosciadium'' within the genus ''Apium'', and this generic name was subsequently established in the literature of the second half of the 19th century and the entire 20th century.<ref name="McDonald-2006" />

The name ''Helosciadium'' is derived from the combination of the Greek words ''hélos'' and ''skiás'', meaning "swamp" and "canopy" respectively, inspired by the habitat occupied by these plants and the type of inflorescence. The specific epithet ''repens'' comes from the [[Latin]] word ''repo'', meaning "creeping" or "trailing".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rejewski |first=Marian |title=Pochodzenie łacińskich nazw roślin polskich: przewodnik botaniczny |date=1996 |publisher=Książka i Wiedza |isbn=978-83-05-12868-1 |location=Warszawa |pages=82, 133 | language=pl}}</ref>

== Threats and protection ==
The species has not been globally assessed for its endangerment status, but almost its entire geographical range is within Europe, where it has been considered [[Near-threatened species|near threatened]] (NT) at the continent scale.<ref name="eunis">{{Cite web |title=Apium repens - (Jacq.) Lag. |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/151923 |access-date=2024-04-08 |website=eunis.eea.europa.eu}}</ref> It is protected by the [[Berne Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats|Berne Convention]] and the [[Habitats Directive]].<ref name="eunis" /><ref name="Piękoś-Mirkowa-2006" /> It is a subject of protection in 167 [[Natura 2000]] sites in the [[European Union]].<ref name="eunis" /> In all countries where the species occurs, it is listed on red lists of threatened species.<ref name="Jansen" /> Among the threatened species of European plants, it ranks third in terms of distribution (measured by the number of countries where it grows).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Sharrock |first1=Suzanne |title=Conserving Europe's threatened plants |last2=Jones |first2=Meirion |publisher=BGCI |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-905164-30-1 |location=Richmond |page=17}}</ref>

This plant has been under strict protection<ref name="Piękoś-Mirkowa-2006" /> in [[Poland]] since 2001.<ref>The Regulation of the Minister of the Environment of 11 September 2001, regarding the list of native plant species occurring in the wild, subject to strict or partial species protection, and the appropriate prohibitions and exceptions from these prohibitions ([https://isap.sejm.gov.pl/isap.nsf/DocDetails.xsp?id=WDU20011061167 Journal of Laws of 2001, No. 106, item 1167]).</ref> Since 2004, it has been under species protection with the reservation that the species requires active protection,<ref>The Regulation of the Minister of the Environment of 9 July 2004, regarding wild plant species subject to protection ([https://isap.sejm.gov.pl/isap.nsf/DocDetails.xsp?id=WDU20041681764 Journal of Laws of 2004, No. 168, item 1764]).</ref> and since 2012, legal protection also applies to activities related to conducting rational agricultural, forestry, or fishing management.<ref>[https://isap.sejm.gov.pl/isap.nsf/DocDetails.xsp?id=WDU20120000081 Journal of Laws of 2012, No. 81] – Regulation of the Minister of the Environment of 5 January 2012, regarding the species protection of plants.</ref><ref>Regulation of the Minister of the Environment of 9 October 2014, regarding the species protection of plants ([https://isap.sejm.gov.pl/isap.nsf/DocDetails.xsp?id=WDU20140001409 Journal of Laws of 2014, No. 1409]).</ref>

The main reasons for the decline of the species at its habitats include the cessation of meadow and pasture use,<ref name="Jansen" /> which leads to the development of tall, competitive meadow vegetation that displaces this heliophilous, low species.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> Another significant problem is the drainage of such habitats, especially eliminating winter water stagnation.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> Excessive grazing can also lead to the disappearance of the creeping marshwort.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> Destruction of lake shores due to tourism and recreation and displacement due to natural [[ecological succession]] by meadow, marsh, or forest vegetation are also considered threats.<ref name="Piękoś-Mirkowa-2006" /> In the British Isles, populations of this species may be threatened by invasions of the alien species ''Crassula helmsii'',<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> and in Central Europe, locally, [[Acorus calamus|sweet flag]] (''Acorus calamus'') poses a problem.<ref name="GIO" /> In Western Europe, potential threats also include hybridization of the species with [[Helosciadium nodiflorum|fool's watercress]] (''Helosciadium nodiflorum'').<ref name="Stroh-2016" />

From climate change models, it follows that a significant area of the current range will be reduced due to forecasted climate changes in the coming decades ([[global warming]]). Outside the climatic optimum of the species, extensive areas will be found in southern Europe, but also in lowlands from France through Germany to Poland. Favorable conditions for the species will arise in higher mountain areas (mainly the [[Alps]] and the [[Carpathian Mountains|Carpathians]]) and in areas under the influence of an oceanic climate in Northern Europe (the central part of [[Great Britain]], the [[Jutland Peninsula]], the central part of the [[Scandinavian Peninsula]]). In Poland, the conditions for the occurrence of the species will worsen in lakeland areas but will be maintained or improved in mountainous and upland areas and on the coast.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-10-09 |title=Apium repens (Jacquin) Lag. |url=https://www.cwrnl.nl/en/cwrnl-1/cwrbyname/apium-repens-jacquin-lag.-1.htm |access-date=2024-04-08 |website=pgrportal.nl |language=en-us}}</ref>

Conservation actions include, among others, creating gaps in dense vegetation patches within the species' habitats, facilitating the germination of its seeds (germination is stimulated by access to light and can occur at different times of the year except winter). Due to the long viability of creeping marshwort's seeds in the soil seed bank, it is possible to restore this species to its habitats if habitat conditions improve (the species has been successfully restored to some sites in Great Britain in this way).<ref name="Burmeier-2008" /><ref name="Jansen" /> Key to the species' conservation is maintaining floods in the winter-spring period and extensive grazing.<ref name="Stroh-2016" /> Effective in creating surrogate sites and reintroductions is introducing seedlings to new locations with suitable habitat conditions.<ref name="Burmeier-2009" /><ref name="Jansen" />

Protective measures involving the collection of plants from nature, their multiplication, and reinforcement of threatened populations, as well as the restoration of vanished sites, have also been successfully carried out in Poland in [[Gniezno]] and in the [[Przemęt Landscape Park]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Selery błotne uratowane |url=http://www.gdos.gov.pl/selery-blotne-uratowane |access-date=2024-04-08 |website=www.gdos.gov.pl |archive-date=2024-04-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240408225023/http://www.gdos.gov.pl/selery-blotne-uratowane |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Properties ==

=== Edible plant ===
Due to the traditional, albeit erroneous, inclusion of this species in the ''[[Apium]]'' genus, this species (and others in the ''Helosciadium'' genus) have likely been attributed with similar nutritional and medicinal properties as [[celery root]], which is a popular vegetable. On the other hand, determining the true relationship and systematic position of this species may not change much in assessing its edibility ([[Berula erecta|lesser water-parsnip]] (''Berula erecta'') from the closest related genus to ''Helosciadium'', is also edible).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Łuczaj |first=Łukasz |title=Dzikie rośliny jadalne Polski: przewodnik survivalowy |date=2004 |publisher=Chemigrafia |isbn=978-83-904633-6-0 |edition=2 |location=Krosno |pages=171, 194}}</ref> The leaves of creeping marshwort have a pleasant, mild taste reminiscent of [[parsley]].<ref name="Grassly-1996" />

The long-standing recognition of creeping marshwort as a species closely related to celeriac has led to initiatives aimed at protecting this species as a genetic reserve for celery.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Frese |first1=Lothar |last2=Bönisch |first2=M. |last3=Herden |first3=Tobias |last4=Zander |first4=M. |last5=Friesen |first5=Nikolai |year=2018 |title=In-situ conservation of species of wild celery – Example for genetic resources of Crop Wild Relatives (CWR) |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325809861 |journal=Naturschutz und Landschaftsplanung |volume=50 |issue=5 |pages=155–163}}</ref>

=== Ornamental plant ===
Due to its prostrate growth habit and its ability to form dense mats in favorable conditions, the plant is used as ground cover in sunny areas along pond banks.<ref name="Hagen-2010">{{Cite book |last1=Hagen |first1=Peter |title=Staw w ogrodzie: budowa, pielęgnacja, rośliny i zwierzęta |last2=Floriańczyk |first2=Barbara |last3=Haberer |first3=Martin |date=2010 |publisher=Klub dla Ciebie - Bauer-Weltbild Media |isbn=978-83-258-0272-1 |location=Warszawa |page=250}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==

=== Propagation ===
Plants of this species can be propagated by division and from seeds.<ref name="Hagen-2010" /> Vegetatively, they can easily be multiplied by dividing the stolons. In an experiment, stolons cut into pieces (each including at least one node) rooted and produced new shoots on average in 86%.<ref name="Jansen" />

In the case of cultivation aimed at increasing the species' resources in nature, especially for creating new replacement habitats, it is recommended to propagate plants from seeds obtained from different populations. This allows increasing the genetic diversity of populations at the established habitats. [[Stratification (seeds)|Stratification]] is recommended, involving storing the seeds in darkness and cool temperatures for two months (e.g., on moist substrate at 4°C). The seeds are then sown on standard horticultural substrate and kept in a moist greenhouse. For obtaining as many seedlings as possible, vegetative division of the obtained plants is recommended. After planting at the target habitats, particularly in areas grazed by animals, it is advisable to fence the newly planted plants in the initial period to allow them to establish well (shortly after transplantation, they are easily pulled out of the ground by foraging animals). It is also optimal to remove competitive plants by planting the creeping marshwort in strips of bare soil. The best results are achieved by planting during humid weather, preferably at the beginning of autumn. In case of drought, significant losses may occur among freshly planted plants. Since losses are usually expected in the first year of cultivation, to obtain a sustainable population, it is recommended to use as much plant material as possible when creating replacement habitats.<ref name="Jansen" />

=== Maintenance ===
To maintain the species, it is necessary to limit competitive vegetation through grazing or mowing and to maintain disturbances in the vegetation at the species' occurrence site (e.g., trampling by animals, flooding, and water stagnation during the winter-spring period).<ref name="Jansen" />
